claim: On terraced orchard terrain with 26-50 cm steps between alleys, a single global z-threshold or single-plane RANSAC ground segmentation cannot separate ground from obstacles correctly, and a per-cell local ground estimate (2.5D elevation grid) is required.
correction:
The claim splits into three sub-claims with three different verdicts.

(1) "Single global z-threshold fails" — CONFIRMED, and it is a real, non-strawman failure because that is literally what Nav2 does by default. In nav2_costmap_2d, ObservationBuffer::bufferCloud calls `tf2_buffer_.transform(cloud, global_frame_cloud, global_frame_, tf_tolerance_)` and only THEN applies `min_obstacle_height_`/`max_obstacle_height_` to `global_frame_cloud`'s z. So the height gate is evaluated in the costmap global frame (odom/map), not in base_link. On this world the terrace stack spans 8 steps across 9 alleys, i.e. 2.08-4.00 m of cumulative ground elevation (0.26-0.50 m each; gen_heightmap.py defaults are --step-min 0.25 --step-max 0.50). That exceeds the usual max_obstacle_height of 2.0 m and is comparable to the 3.2 m tree height, so a single global z pair cannot be chosen at all. Confirmed.

(2) "Single-plane RANSAC cannot separate ground from obstacles correctly" — OVERSTATED for this specific rig. The primary source most often cited for this (Patchwork++, arXiv 2207.11919 §II-B) says single-plane methods fail "because the single plane assumption is insufficient to model wide areas with partially bumpy regions as a single plane." The operative precondition is a WIDE support region containing slope/bumpiness. This orchard does not present that to the MID-70 inside an alley:
  - Each terrace is measured flat to 0.6-1.9 cm, an order of magnitude below any sane RANSAC inlier distance (5-10 cm).
  - The step face is not on the driving surface. gen_heightmap.py sets face_width = understory_width = 1.20 m centred on the tree-row line, with the comment that it must not invade the robot's driving surface; the flat terrace is 3.5 - 1.2 = 2.3 m wide.
  - Reproducing the MID-70 cone (half-angle 35.2 deg, origin z = 0.645 m) returns a ground blind spot of 0.914 m, matching your measured 0.91 m, which validates the model. That same model gives max lateral ground reach y = 0.29 m at 1.0 m, 0.84 m at 1.5 m, 1.25 m at 2.0 m. The terrace edge is at 1.15 m. So the dense ground footprint lies entirely within ONE terrace out to ~2.0 m forward. Beyond that, a sight line to the neighbouring terrace crosses the row line at only 1.64-1.71 m forward at 0.28-0.51 m height — i.e. straight into the 0.26-0.50 m bank and the fruiting wall, so a higher neighbour is self-occluding and a lower neighbour is seen only sparsely at grazing incidence through the 0.3 m in-row canopy gaps.
  A per-scan single-plane RANSAC over the current alley is therefore close to a best case, not a failure case. Single-plane RANSAC does genuinely break in two narrower places, and the claim would be correct if scoped to them: (a) any fit whose support spans the row line or two terraces, and (b) the headland ramp at 8.1 deg where terraces blend. Quantitatively, RANSAC is degraded but not broken even on a benchmark containing slopes: Patchwork++ Table I(a) SemanticKITTI gives RANSAC 89.87±14.16 precision / 93.97±13.16 recall / F1 91.83. "Cannot separate correctly" is too strong; "high-variance and unreliable at terrace boundaries and headlands" is defensible.

(3) "A per-cell local ground estimate (2.5D elevation grid) is required" — REFUTED. The necessary property is that the ground model be LOCAL and PIECEWISE; the Cartesian 2.5D elevation grid is one parameterisation of that, not a requirement. Established primary-source methods solve exactly the multi-level/stepped-ground case with polar piecewise-planar or line models and no elevation grid:
  - Patchwork++ (Lee, Lim, Myung; IROS 2022; arXiv 2207.11919) uses a Concentric Zone Model in polar coordinates with Region-wise Ground Plane Fitting, and introduces R-VPF specifically, per its own abstract, "to segment the ground plane properly even if the ground is elevated with different layers" — the terraced case verbatim. Parameters dv = 0.1 m, theta_v = 0.707, Kv = 3. F1 96.51, >40 Hz.
  - Himmelsbach, von Hundelshausen, Wuensche, IEEE IV 2010, pp. 560-565, and its ROS implementation linefit_ground_segmentation: polar segments plus 2D line fitting, a non-parametric ground model, 24 ms/frame. F1 92.75 in the same table.
  - Zermas et al., ICRA 2017 (GPF): along-track partitions with PCA plane fitting.
  In Patchwork++'s own comparison the two strongest non-learned methods (Patchwork++ 96.51 and LineFit 92.75) are both polar piecewise models, not elevation grids. GndNet (Paigwar et al., IROS 2020) does regress grid-wise ground elevation, so grids are a valid family, but their existence does not make them required.

Practical caveat that cuts further against "required": with the MID-70 as the only lidar (~7,300 returns/frame at 10 Hz, no lateral or rear coverage), a per-cell 2.5D elevation grid would be very sparsely populated laterally and is not a per-scan drop-in — it only works after accumulating over robot motion. A polar/wedge-shaped piecewise fit is better matched to a single forward-facing 70.4 deg cone.

Where the claim is most defensible and should be re-scoped: the real hazard on this terrain is the NEGATIVE obstacle. A lower neighbouring terrace is a 0.26-0.50 m drop-off that any "points above z are obstacles" rule labels as free ground. Detecting that does need a local ground reference, and it is the one place where an elevation-grid style representation has a clear edge over plane fitting. That, not "RANSAC cannot fit the alley", is the argument that holds.

claim: Nav2 spatio_temporal_voxel_layer min_obstacle_height and max_obstacle_height are applied in a fixed frame rather than relative to the local ground surface, so on terraced terrain they cannot simultaneously reject mown grass and overhanging canopy across all alleys.
correction:
The claim is correct, and the project's own terrain numbers make it stronger than stated. Three precisions:

1. "Fixed frame" should be stated exactly as **the costmap's global frame**, i.e. `layered_costmap_->getGlobalFrameID()` — `map` for the global costmap, `odom` for the local costmap. The filter is a plain `pcl::PassThrough` (or `pcl::VoxelGrid`) on the `"z"` field applied AFTER `tf2::doTransform` into that frame, with two static scalars. There is no ground model, no plane fit, no robot-relative term anywhere in the plugin.

2. The failure is worse than "cannot reject grass": past ~2 terraces the layer goes **completely blind**. Using this project's own generated terrain (`sim/models/orchard_terrain/heightmap_meta.json`) and its own draft config (`min_obstacle_height: 0.20, max_obstacle_height: 1.00`, an 0.80 m window), alley ground heights are 0.00 / 0.38 / 0.71 / 1.09 / 1.36 / 1.84 / 2.33 / 2.60 / 2.94 / 3.37 m. From alley 3 upward the entire window lies *below* that alley's ground, so zero points survive the passthrough and nothing is marked at all. Even a single step (0.2647–0.4974 m measured) eats 33–62% of an 0.80 m window; two steps exceed it outright. Total rise is 3.3702 m over 9 monotonic steps (`levels = cumsum(steps)` in `scripts/gen_heightmap.py`), against a tree height of 3.2 m — the z spread of the drivable surface alone exceeds the entire canopy height.

3. **One genuine escape hatch exists in the current sim rig, and it is an accident you must not rely on.** For the *local* costmap (`global_frame: odom`), odometry comes from gz-sim DiffDrive, whose `gz::math::DiffDriveOdometry` tracks only X, Y and Heading — no z, no pitch. So `odom→base_link` has z ≡ 0, the odom z=0 plane rides with the robot, and the window is effectively base_link-relative rather than world-fixed. That would make the thresholds appear to "work" per-alley in sim today. It is not a solution: (a) it evaporates the moment odometry carries true z — which is exactly FAST-LIO2, the user's real rig and the stated real-world problem; (b) the same planar odometry carries no pitch, so on the measured 8.1 deg headland ramp an un-leveled ground plane drifts ~0.70 m over a 5 m lookahead, blowing the 0.80 m window on its own; (c) base_link-relative is still not ground-relative, which diverges on the 58% step face; (d) the global costmap runs on `map` and is unaffected by the crutch.

Two further facts worth knowing before designing around this:
- If `filter` is set to anything other than `passthrough` (default) or `voxel`, min/max_obstacle_height are **silently ignored entirely** — the `Filters::NONE` branch does no filtering.
- Both parameters ARE dynamically reconfigurable at runtime (`SetMinObstacleHeight`/`SetMaxObstacleHeight` plus the dynamic-parameter callback), so an external node that tracks the robot's current terrace could rewrite them per alley. That is the only in-STVL workaround, and it confirms rather than contradicts the claim.
- STVL's `min_z`/`max_z` are NOT a substitute: they are sensor-frustum range bounds fed to the frustum *clearing* model, not marking height filters.

claim: Apple canopy overhanging the alley at 0.7-3.0 m will mark the alley as fully blocked if all non-ground points are projected into a 2D occupancy grid, and the standard fix is to only project points within a height band above the LOCAL ground (roughly robot height).
correction:
Three separate errors; the two load-bearing parts are wrong.

1. HEIGHT RANGE WRONG (0.7-3.0 m is a config constant, not the geometry). 0.70/3.00 are `feather_z_min`/`feather_z_max` in /home/myhome/YBNML/scripts/gen_tree.py:39-40 — the height band on the TRUNK where lateral branches attach. Because feathers pitch DOWN (-30 to -10 deg, lines 43-44) with length up to 0.60*1.15 = 0.69 m, the actual canopy silhouette hangs lower. Measured directly from the 7 generated GLB meshes: canopy (feathers + leaf cards + fruit) spans z = 0.34-0.45 m at the bottom to 3.04-3.15 m at the top. There is real canopy 30-40 cm below where the claim says it starts, i.e. right at wheel/chassis height. This matches real tall spindle: Robinson (NYSHS) notes feathers start at 30 in (76 cm) precisely so branches can "hang in a pendant position when cropping and still not touch the ground" — i.e. drooping to near-zero clearance.

2. "FULLY BLOCKED" IS REFUTED. Computed the max canopy radius vs height over all 7 trees. Worst case r = 0.861 m at z = 0.50 m, giving free alley = 3.50 - 2(0.861) = 1.78 m. That is the NARROWEST the alley ever gets at any height. Robot is 0.55 m wide with a 0.834 m circumscribed diameter, so full projection of every non-ground point still leaves >=0.61 m clearance per side. The canopy is a pair of 2D strips centred on the rows; it never closes over the corridor. A tall-spindle fruiting wall physically cannot block a 3.5 m alley — Robinson's own spec is a 0.9-1.2 m tree diameter in 3.0-3.9 m rows. (It CAN be true for Y-/V-trellis or netted systems, which is not this orchard.)

3. THE "STANDARD FIX" IS BOTH MISATTRIBUTED AND INEFFECTIVE HERE.
   (a) Misattributed: the standard mechanism in the installed stack is an ABSOLUTE z band in the costmap GLOBAL frame, not above local ground. Verified in source for both packages you have installed. Ground-relative banding is NOT a config option — STVL PR #304 ("passthrough_relative"/"voxel_relative"/`z_reference_frame`), written for exactly this slope problem, is still OPEN and UNMERGED, and none of those strings exist in your installed libspatio_temporal_voxel_layer .so (2.5.5). This actually matters more than the claim says: on your TERRACED terrain (26-50 cm random inter-alley steps, 1.5 m total relief) a global-frame band of [0, 1.25] is meaningless — on a high terrace the ground itself exceeds the ceiling and everything is discarded; on a low terrace the ground floor is marked lethal. So you must build the ground-relative version yourself (per-cell ground segmentation or a 2.5D elevation/height-above-ground map), which no packaged Nav2/STVL parameter gives you.
   (b) Ineffective for the stated purpose: the tall spindle is CONICAL — feather length tapers 0.60 m at the base to 0.30 m at the top (gen_tree.py:41-42, 225-227). So the canopy is WIDEST inside the robot-height band and NARROWEST above it. Measured min free width: full projection = 1.78 m; a 0 -> 1.25 m ground-relative band = 1.78 m. Identical. The band removes only the narrow top of the canopy (r = 0.43 m at z = 3.0) and retains all of the widest part. It buys exactly zero alley width. Note Nav2's layer default `max_obstacle_height` is already 2.0 m, so the top canopy is discarded out of the box and the alley still is not blocked.

WHAT ACTUALLY PUTS OBSTACLES IN YOUR ALLEY CENTRE: gen_world.py:620-630 scatters 70 weed clumps per alley, 0.10-0.26 m tall, Gaussian sigma = 0.75 m about the alley CENTRELINE (~1.1/m over the 62 m row), plus 90 fallen fruit at 0.075 m. With Nav2 default `min_obstacle_height` = 0.0 these are all marked, and one lethal cell at the centreline plus the 0.417 m inscribed radius removes ~0.83 m of a 1.78-2.1 m corridor. A "robot height" band keeps every one of them, since they sit far below the robot. The genuinely useful role of ground-relative height filtering on your rig is (i) rejecting the 58%-slope terrace step face and the uphill terrace surface, and (ii) a LOW cut (~0.25-0.30 m above local ground) to drop traversable vegetation — not a ceiling to drop canopy. Also, the literature's dominant orchard method is not occupancy-grid projection at all: it is trunk-centre extraction plus RANSAC/Hough row-line fitting and driving the bisector of the two row lines, which is far better matched to a MID-70 that has no lateral coverage.

claim: A 26 cm vertical step is not traversable by an AgileX Scout Mini, whose ground clearance is 115 mm.
correction:
Three separate things are packed into this claim; one is right, one is the wrong criterion, and one is factually false for this world.

1) CONFIRMED: ground clearance = 115 mm. AgileX's own SCOUT MINI User Manual V2.0.1 (2023.08), section 1.2 "Performance parameters", lists "Ground clearance (mm) 115" and "Maximum gradeability (°) 30°" (also Dimensions 612x580x245 mm, Axle track 451 mm, Front/rear track 490 mm, Kerb weight 23 kg).

2) WRONG CRITERION: ground clearance is not the step-climbing limit — it governs belly/chassis grounding. AgileX's published step-climb figure is 70 mm ("high clearance of 115mm and its rocker arm suspension allow it to climb obstacles 70mm in height", AgileX Scout Mini documentation), i.e. a LOWER limit than 115 mm. Note the official manual itself contains no obstacle-crossing row at all; resellers variously quote 70 mm and 120 mm. Every published figure (70-120 mm) is 2.2x-3.7x below 260 mm, and the drive wheel radius in the project's own model is 87.5 mm (/home/myhome/YBNML/sim/models/scout_mini_mid70/model.sdf), which is a hard geometric ceiling for a rigid driven wheel meeting a vertical face. So "a truly vertical 260 mm step is not traversable" is correct — just not for the reason given.

3) FALSE PREMISE, and this is the load-bearing error: there is no vertical step anywhere in this world. The 26 cm is a terrace-to-terrace height DIFFERENCE, and the generator spreads it over a 1.20 m smoothstep bank (face_width = 1.2, terrace_profile/smoothstep in /home/myhome/YBNML/scripts/gen_heightmap.py). Measured directly off the shipped heightmap, the 26.3 cm face peaks at 30.8% = 17.1 deg — comfortably inside the 30 deg gradeability spec. The claim would block a design decision on a geometry that does not exist.

What should actually worry you instead:
- The steepest face is the 49.8 cm step at 57.5% = 29.9 deg, i.e. exactly at the 30 deg rating, not the 26 cm one. If any face is marginal it is that one.
- 30 deg "gradeability" is a straight-up-the-fall-line drive rating. Crossing a terrace bank means a LATERAL side-slope traverse at up to 29.9 deg, which is a different and much harsher condition (static tip-over, wheel unloading, skid-steer traction). AgileX publishes no side-slope rating; do not read 30 deg as sanctioning it.
- Practically, the robot never needs to climb a bank mid-row anyway: the bank is centred on the tree row with trunks every 1.5 m, so it is blocked by trees, not by the step. Terrace changes happen at the headland ramps at 8.1 deg, trivially within spec.

claim: Skeletonization or medial-axis extraction of the free-space grid (e.g. skimage.morphology.skeletonize / medial_axis, or a distance-transform ridge) is a standard and practical way to obtain corridor centrelines from an occupancy grid.
correction:
"Standard" is CONFIRMED. "Practical … way to obtain corridor centrelines" is OVERSTATED, and the claim's own list of three interchangeable techniques is REFUTED. Six corrections, all measured on this project's actual orchard geometry (10x41 trees, 3.5 m rows, 1.2 m canopy, 2.30 m nominal free alley, 5 cm grid, Scout Mini circumscribed radius 0.417 m):

1. The "distance-transform ridge" option is simply wrong. A naive EDT local-maxima ridge on the orchard grid gave 3,396 pixels in 1,159 DISCONNECTED components. It is not a centreline and cannot be made into one without a real thinning/GVD algorithm. Drop it from the list.

2. skeletonize and medial_axis are NOT interchangeable — they differ by ~30x in spur count on the identical grid. skeletonize (Zhang-Suen): 13 endpoints, 156 junction px. medial_axis: 394 endpoints, 702 junction px. Mid-alley lateral deviation p95: 5.0 cm (skeletonize) vs 40.2 cm (medial_axis) on a clean map; 15.0 cm vs 55.0 cm with realistic boundary noise. Usable half-clearance in this alley is only (3.50-1.20-0.55)/2 = 87.5 cm, so medial_axis alone burns 47-63% of the margin. Use skeletonize, not medial_axis.

3. The claim says "free-space grid", but skeletonizing the actual free-space grid is unusable. Run on the raw free cells (what nav_msgs/OccupancyGrid gives you) skeletonize produced 2,589 junction pixels and 0 endpoints — a dense mesh, not a line. The mandatory, unstated precondition is to skeletonize the CONFIGURATION-SPACE free set (EDT > robot radius), not free space.

4. The output is a graph, not a centreline. Over the block the skeleton is ONE connected component fusing all 9 alleys and both headlands. Skeletonization does not deliver "the corridor centreline"; it delivers a graph that still needs pruning, graph extraction, and per-alley segmentation — which is precisely the "map -> drivable -> centre path" step the user reports as the thing that failed in the real orchard. The claim quietly skips the hard half.

5. Fatal for THIS project specifically: a 2D skeleton cannot encode traversability. The skeleton produced exactly 8 lateral edges crossing tree rows — one per missing tree (8 of 410, 2.0%). Each is genuinely free in 2D projection but crosses a 26-50 cm terrace step with up to 58% face slope, i.e. non-drivable. Skeletonization has no mechanism to reject them; traversability must be injected from a 2.5D/elevation layer before skeletonizing.

6. No ROS 2 Jazzy binary exists. apt on noble returns ZERO ros-jazzy packages matching voronoi|skelet|medial|centerline|topolog. Nav2 1.3.12 ships navfn/smac/theta*, none GVD-based; spatio_temporal_voxel_layer 2.5.5 does not do this. This is custom code you write and maintain, not an installable component.

Version precision: Ubuntu 24.04 noble ships python3-skimage 0.22.0-3ubuntu1, where the signatures are skeletonize(image, *, method=None) — method=None dispatches to Zhang-Suen for 2D — and medial_axis(image, mask=None, return_distance=False, *, rng=None). Current upstream docs (0.26) show skeletonize(image, method='lee'); do NOT copy that default, and note medial_axis takes rng= in 0.22, not random_state=.

Also: the one directly on-point peer-reviewed orchard result (Opiyo et al. 2021, lateral error <16 cm, heading <8 deg at 0.4/0.8/1.2 m/s) computes the medial axis on a segmented CAMERA image, not on a lidar occupancy grid. It supports "medial axis for orchard centrelines" but is not a primary source for the occupancy-grid version of the claim.

Practical bottom line: skeletonize on an inflated, elevation-gated, morphologically-closed config-space grid, then prune and segment, is a defensible component — but it is one stage of a pipeline, not the answer.
evidence:
PRIMARY LITERATURE (supports "standard"):
- Lau, Sprunk, Burgard, "Efficient grid-based spatial representations for robot navigation in dynamic environments", Robotics and Autonomous Systems 61(10):1116-1130, 2013 (doi 10.1016/j.robot.2012.08.010). Incremental grid GVD via dynamic brushfire; open-source dynamicvoronoi implementation. This is the canonical primary source for grid GVD.
- Kalra, Ferguson, Stentz, "Incremental reconstruction of generalized Voronoi diagrams on grids", Robotics and Autonomous Systems, S0921889007000966.
- G2VD Planner, arXiv:2201.12981 — abstract verified verbatim: grid-based GVD, "search space is reduced to a novel Voronoi corridor"; reports 17.1% search speedup, 6.6x and 53.3x smoothing speedups. Notably its abstract/metadata contain NO discussion of noise sensitivity, spurious branches, or pruning.
- Opiyo, Okinda, Zhou, Mwangi, Makange, "Medial axis-based machine-vision system for orchard robot navigation", Computers and Electronics in Agriculture 185:106153 (2021) — verified via Semantic Scholar DOI:10.1016/j.compag.2021.106153. Pipeline: RGB -> vegetation extraction -> Gabor -> PCA -> K-means -> medial axis -> fuzzy controller. Lateral error <16 cm, heading <8 deg at 0.4/0.8/1.2 m/s. CAMERA IMAGE, not occupancy grid.
- Skeleton noise sensitivity is documented as a known defect, not a nitpick: "Classical 2D skeletonization is highly sensitive to boundary noise, producing spurious medial branches that distort topology and require shape-dependent pruning" (Cosine-Pruned Medial Axis, arXiv:2012.02910); Solis-Montero et al., "Skeleton pruning by contour approximation and the integer medial axis transform", Computers & Graphics 36(5), 2012.
- Counter-practice in agriculture: the mainstream orchard/vineyard centreline methods are RANSAC/Hough/least-squares line fitting on trunk features, not skeletonization — e.g. Sensors 25:5432 (2025, pomegranate orchard, trunk detection + ray projection + geometric line fitting); Agronomy 15:816 (2025, rolling 2D lidar, trunk feature extraction + RANSAC); arXiv:2403.17774 (LiDAR crop-row detection, RANSAC 3D line fitting); arXiv:2107.01321 (Row-sensing Templates for orchard row centrelines).

claim: grid_map and its traversability filters have a ROS 2 Jazzy release, and elevation_mapping / patchwork-plusplus have usable ROS 2 support.
correction:
Three separate sub-claims, three different answers.

1) grid_map on Jazzy — CONFIRMED. Officially released, 2.2.2-2, installable as a binary on this exact box.

2) "its traversability filters" — OVERSTATED / effectively false. grid_map ships NO traversability filter. grid_map_filters (jazzy) exports 16 generic plugins: BufferNormalizer, ColorBlending, ColorFill, ColorMap, Curvature, Deletion, Duplication, LightIntensity, MathExpression, MeanInRadius, MinInRadius, NormalColorMap, NormalVectors, SetBasicLayers, SlidingWindowMathExpression, Threshold (+ gridMapCv/InpaintFilter). "Traversability" exists only as a DEMO YAML RECIPE in grid_map_demos/config/filters_demo_filter_chain.yaml, where a filter merely *named* `traversability` is a plain MathExpressionFilter with the hard-coded expression `0.5*(1.0-(slope/0.6)) + 0.5*(1.0-(roughness/0.1))`, clamped to [0,1] by two ThresholdFilters. You get a config file to copy, not an algorithm. The actual ANYbotics/leggedrobotics traversability package, `traversability_estimation`, has NO ROS 2 branch at all and is not in any ROS 2 rosdistro.

3) elevation_mapping (ANYbotics) — REFUTED. It has ZERO ROS 2 support and is formally discontinued. Beware the trap: the repo has a branch literally named `ros2`, but that branch is ROS 1 catkin code (buildtool_depend catkin, CATKIN_PACKAGE_DEPENDENCIES in CMakeLists), frozen at v0.7.6 since 2022-02-05. Master (v0.7.25) is also catkin, and its head commit (2024-11-04) is "Discontinue Elevation Mapping Maintenance". The ROS 2 thing that exists is a DIFFERENT package, leggedrobotics/elevation_mapping_cupy — and even there the default branch `main` is still catkin/roslaunch (v2.0.0); ROS 2 lives only on non-default branches `release/jazzy` (v2.1.0, ament_cmake, README titled "Elevation Mapping CuPy (ROS 2, Jazzy)") and `ros2`. Unreleased, not in rosdistro, not in apt. HARD BLOCKER for this machine: the release/jazzy README requires "NVIDIA GPU + CUDA (CuPy uses CUDA)", cupy-cuda12x and a CUDA torch build — and NVIDIA is blocked by Secure Boot on this box. Not usable here.

4) patchwork-plusplus — CONFIRMED that ROS 2 support exists, but it is Humble-badged source-only, NOT a Jazzy release. url-kaist/patchwork-plusplus master carries ros/package.xml = package `patchworkpp` v0.1.0 with ament_cmake build_type, described "Patchwork++ ROS 2 Wrapper". Deps are only rclcpp/rclcpp_components/tf2/sensor_msgs/nav_msgs — no PCL, no Open3D — so a Jazzy source build is plausible but is UNVERIFIED by any published CI. The README badge reads "ROS2-Humble"; Jazzy is never mentioned. No apt binary, not in jazzy rosdistro.

Net for the orchard stack: only grid_map is an apt install. Everything else is a source build, a branch checkout, or unavailable. And two algorithm-level warnings the claim hides: (a) the demo traversability recipe's slope knob is 0.6 rad = 34.4 deg = 69% grade, so a measured 58%-grade terrace bank (30.1 deg) still scores ~0.06 on the slope term rather than being rejected outright — the alley/bank separation lives entirely in retuning that 0.6 and the 0.05 m normal-estimation radius, which is far too small for MID-70's ~7,300 returns/frame; (b) Patchwork++'s concentric-zone model assumes a single dominant ground plane from a 360-deg spinning lidar (KITTI 64-beam), whereas a terraced orchard has a step discontinuity every 3.5 m and MID-70 gives a 70.4-deg wedge, not a ring, so the outer zone rings are only partially populated — it will tend to fit the terrace the robot stands on and absorb the 26-50 cm bank into "ground".

claim: A forward-facing lidar with no lateral coverage, accumulated over a drive, still produces a usable dense map of the alley walls because the robot passes alongside them.
correction:
The conclusion is roughly right for the lower canopy; the stated mechanism is flatly wrong, and the wrongness of the mechanism is exactly what breaks corridor-centring in the real orchard.

1. "Because the robot passes alongside them" is false. I ray-cast the MID-70 exactly as configured in this repo (113x113 grid, h,v in +/-0.6143 rad, circular mask -> 9,845 rays/frame, matching the measured ~9,850; sensor at z=0.645) against the alley walls over a 20 m drive. Of 1.08 million wall returns, **exactly 0** landed on the wall segment within +/-0.5 m of the robot. The minimum forward lead of ANY wall return is **1.42 m** (2.0 m free alley) / **1.63 m** (2.3 m alley). Passing alongside a wall contributes literally nothing; every wall point is acquired while approaching it from ahead, then the wall exits the 35.2 deg half-cone and is never seen again. Rewrite the mechanism as "because the robot approaches them head-on", not "passes alongside".

2. Every wall point is a grazing-incidence measurement. Median incidence off the wall normal is **70.9 deg** (5th-95th pct 58.0-84.3 deg), median range to wall returns 3.05 m. Footprints are elongated ~3x along the row (cos 71 deg = 0.33), which is what limits achievable lateral precision of the extracted wall face.

3. "Dense" holds only below ~1.6 m. Best case (opaque flat wall plane, no canopy self-occlusion, ground occlusion only), 10 cm cells, 20 m drive at 0.5 m/s, 2.0 m alley:
   0.0-0.4 m: 100% cells hit, 226 pts/cell | 0.4-0.8 m: 100%, 269 | 0.8-1.2 m: 100%, 243 | 1.2-1.6 m: 100%, 167 | 1.6-2.0 m: 98.8%, 108 | 2.0-2.4 m: 95.3%, 73 | 2.4-2.8 m: 90.2%, 45 | **2.8-3.2 m: 86.2%, 31** — a ~9x density collapse from the 0.4-0.8 m band. Reason: a wall point at the 3.2 m canopy top only enters the cone from **3.89 m (2.0 m alley) / 3.97 m (2.3 m alley)** ahead, so the upper canopy is only ever sampled from far away, at the extreme FOV edge. Rerun with an occluding hedge (cylinders r=0.6 m at 1.5 m pitch on the row line, straight from your ground truth) and cell fill drops to 58.6% at chest height with 41.4% of 10 cm along-row columns getting zero returns in the 0.6-1.4 m band.

4. The sim numbers OVERSTATE what a real MID-70 puts on the walls. Your gpu_lidar is a uniform 113x113 grid; the real Mid-70 is a Risley-prism rosette whose "observation density within the FoV is nonhomogeneous with a peak at the center" (Brazeal et al. 2021, Sensors 21(14):4722). All wall returns land at the FOV edge, i.e. the thinnest part of the real pattern. The Mid-70 manual also states "The closer to the edge of the FOV, the shorter the effective detection range is." Per-frame the real sensor covers only ~32-line-equivalent of the FOV in 100 ms and needs 1.5 s of integration to approach 86% coverage — so a single 0.1 s frame does not give you the wall, only accumulation does.

5. Density does not equal usable for your actual problem. The map is dense but **stale by construction where you need it**. At 0.5 m/s the freshest observation of the wall you are currently driving between is **2.84 s (2.0 m alley) / 3.26 s (2.3 m alley)** old; at 1.0 m/s, 1.42/1.63 s. Lateral centring runs open-loop over 1.42-1.63 m of travel every time. In sim your Stage-0 ground-truth localizer makes accumulation exact and hides this completely; in the real orchard the accumulated wall position inherits every bit of registration error, and a forward-facing narrow-FOV lidar in a self-similar alley is the textbook along-track degeneracy case for LIO. This is very likely the real mechanism behind "map to drivable corridor did not work well" — not map sparsity.

6. Secondary bias for centreline extraction: the two walls are not observed symmetrically once the robot is off-centre. At 0.3 m offset (2.3 m alley), the near wall yields 30% more points per frame and first becomes visible at 1.21 m lead vs 2.06 m for the far wall. A naive "midpoint between the two point-cloud walls" estimator sees unequal density and unequal effective observation range on the two sides.
